senses: Prone to sneeze with little (if any) nasal agitation.
Characterised by sneezes.
Resembling a sneeze.
ety: From Middle English fnesy, equivalent to sneeze + -y. For change of initial f to s see sneeze.
examples: There was a sneezy sound from behind the hedge.

senses: Having an increased tendency to clot.
Cooking equipment intended for use inside an oven.
A person who works or advocates for liberation.
A person in favour of church disestablishment.
examples: Mozambican Lina Magaia is a leading thinker in the struggle for black independence in southern Africa. She is a fighter, an agronomist, an author, an administrator, a liberationist, and a mother.

senses: A police official in the Mughal Empire and the British Raj.
A spirit or monster in Maori mythology, especially one that dwells in the water.
A person who embodies the spirit of a taniwha.
Leather from the skin of a female deer or sheep.
The hide of a doe, as opposed to a buck.
A glove made of doeskin leather.
A very soft, close-napped fabric, especially of high quality.
examples: He was dressed in shirt of doeskin, / White and soft, and fringed with ermine, / All inwrought with beads of wampum...
A long knife was in the doeskin belt that supported the doeskin skirt tightly about her lithe limbs.
Frequently, doeskins had a higher value in trade than the skins of bucks, as they were considered of finer quality.

senses: Favorable; beneficent.
A high-energy particle accelerator.
A horse of western North America that is wild or not fully broken.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish bronco (“rough”), 19th c. which in Mexican usage also describes a horse that has not been broken and is still wild.

senses: Eyeliner when used on men; usually associated with the goth and emo subcultures.
examples: Trevor looks kind of emo, rail thin, dark hair, guyliner, wears black all the time.

senses: A string of oakum used in calking.
ety: English dialect word for a small plug, using -et (“diminutive suffix”).

senses: A flat Roman wall tile with roughened surface, used as a base for plasterwork.
Dormitory rules governing visits from members of the opposite sex.
Wearing a yoke.
The action of blocking or banning a user, account, or IP address from editing or other actions for an indefinite length of time.
examples: An indef seems the only way to stem the flow of disruption from this user.

senses: An electronic device that uses sonar to measure water depth and shows outlines of fish and bottom features on a LCD or CRT screen
Capable of being ionized
A pathogenic bacterium (Neisseria meningitidis), common cause of cerebrospinal meningitis
A plastic resin used to make packaging films.
ety: From a trade name coined by the Dow Chemical Co. for a number of monomers and polymers made from vinylidene chloride (especially polyvinylidene chloride).

senses: One who shanks a golf ball.
One who glues the shank into a shoe.
examples: Littler said he didn't shank it; rather he called it a soft pop-up, but us old hard-core shankers weren't so generous .

senses: A person who selects targets (typically for a remote weapons system).
A stiff, cylindrical military dress hat with a metal plate in front, a short visor, and a plume.
A bearskin or busby.
ety: Borrowed from French shako, from Hungarian csákó (“cylindrical military dress hat worn by the Hungarian hussars from the 18th century to World War I”).

senses: Capable of being fixed, repairable.
Sexual intercourse, especially that involving penile–vaginal penetration.
A slice of meat pounded thin and grilled.
ety: Borrowed from French paillard in the 1970s, from the name of a restaurant in Paris, from its proprietor's surname, Paillard.

senses: An SI unit of time equal to 10⁻⁹ seconds. Symbol: ns
An extremely short period of time; an instant.
examples: I just know that the nanosecond I take my eyes off my phone, somebody's going to steal it.

senses: Capable of being repressed, controlled, suppressed or limited.
A Eurasian rose (Rosa rubiginosa, syn. Rosa eglanteria), having prickly stems, fragrant leaves, pink flowers and red hips.
ety: From French églantine, Middle English eglentyn, from Old French aiglantin (adj.), from Old French aiglent (“sweetbrier”), from Latin aculentus (with the ending of spinulentus (“thorny, prickly”)), from aculeus (“prickle”), from acus (“needle”).

senses: A member of the Girl Scouts of the USA of a rank between junior and senior.
Who enjoys being in crowds and socializing.
ety: First attested in 1688; borrowed from Latin gregārius, see -ious.

senses: A set of software tools used by a third party to gain unauthorized access to a computer system and control the system while concealing itself from the user.
Having a variable focal length, with focus that changes in synchronization.
Synonym of freeze-drying.
ety: First use appears c. 1894 in the US. lyo- + philos + -ization (alternatively analyzed as lyophilize + -ation), from Ancient Greek λύω (lúō, “to loosen, to dissolve”) + φίλος (phílos, “beloved”) + -ίζειν (-ízein) + Latin -ātiō, due to the dried product being able to rapidly reabsorb the solvent and restore the original substance, hence “lyophil” (solvent-loving). Popularized from 1960 by Louis R. Rey. Cognates exist in other European languages by means of the same construction.

senses: To combine two waves of identical frequency.
A crossbeam.
A section formed by crossbeams.
A wooden frame to confine unruly horses while they are shod.
ety: From Middle English trave, from Middle French trave, from Latin trabem, accusative of trabs (“beam, thing made using beams”).

senses: Yielding or containing calcium, calcium carbonate or calcite.
A kind of green tea from Japan, differing from sencha in being grown in the shade.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 玉露 (literally “jade dew”).

senses: A loose-fitting, ankle-length hooded robe worn by men in North Africa.
ety: From French djellaba, from Algerian Arabic جلابة (jallāba).
examples: Dignified gentlemen in sober djellabas, of excellent cut and material, their wives in equally sober djellabas, sat in the tea shops with their children and servants, sipping mint tea.

senses: The probit function, the inverse of the standard normal cumulative distribution function.
ety: Blend of probability + unit. Coined by American statistician Chester Ittner Bliss in 1934: “These arbitrary probability units have been termed ‘probits’…”

senses: An official authorization given by a government to a consul etc.
